back: Planning how to communicate with stakeholders inside and outside the team; aligned with the stakeholder engagement plan.
How, when and by whom information is administered and disseminated. A dynamic document, updated as the project changes.
Requirements, content and format, escalation processes, reasons, frequency, sender, who authorizes confidential releases, recipients, methods.
Finds stakeholders' information needs by combining the type and format of information with its value.
Urgency, availability and reliability, ease of use, project environment (virtual, time zones, languages), sensitivity of the information.
Real-time, multidirectional exchange: meetings, phone calls, instant messaging, videoconferencing.
Sent to specific recipients: letters, memos, reports, emails. Ensures distribution, not understanding.
Accessed at the recipient's discretion: portals, intranets, eLearning, lessons learned databases. For large information sets or audiences.
Interpersonal (individuals), small group (three to six), public (speaker to audience), mass (large, sometimes anonymous audience).
Encode, transmit (noise may interfere), decode. Ensures delivery, not understanding.
Adds acknowledge (receipt only) and feedback/response, to ensure the message is understood.
Sender: clear, complete message, confirm correct interpretation. Receiver: receive in full, interpret correctly, acknowledge or respond.
Anything that compromises understanding: distraction, different perceptions, lack of knowledge or interest, emotions, culture, biases.
Ensures the information needs of the project and stakeholders are met; key benefit: the optimal information flow.
Highly visible displays, such as task boards, that let anyone compare actual with expected performance.
Start small and evolve; visualize openly; review and act; decommission low-value metrics.
Collecting and distributing information adapted in level, format and detail to each stakeholder; regularly or by exception.
The project's current status: progress since the last report and forecasts for cost and schedule.
Work performance information compiled to generate decisions, actions or awareness: status reports, EV graphs, burndowns, risk summaries.
Charts of progress against key measures, with drill-down; often RAG stoplights, with text explaining measures outside thresholds.
Probabilistic forecasts from throughput and item counts, shown as ranges or confidence curves, never single-point commitments.

front: Three core components of effective governance
back: Target metrics aligned with strategy; signaling mechanisms (leading indicators); feedback mechanisms for decision-makers.
Show trends before variances cross thresholds; preferred. Examples: items in progress, no risk process, unengaged stakeholders.
Report what has happened; easier to measure. Examples: deliverables completed, schedule or cost variance, resources used.
